newsitem.title: UK: UK Air cargo exports at 1996 high.
newsitem.headline: UK Air cargo exports at 1996 high.

text.p: Mid-October air cargo exports from the UK are at the highest levels seen so far this year driven by both seasonal factors and firm demand, with rates hardening although few formal tariff increases have been seen, a Reuters survey showed.
Carriers are increasingly weighing the impact of sharply higher jet fuel prices on cargo rates and surcharges cannot be ruled out, industry sources added.

Earlier on Wednesday British Airways said it was raising passenger fares to Europe by an average of 2.5 percent in mid-October due to the fuel situation, and was considering increases on long-haul routes. KLM Royal Dutch Airlines said a definite decision on higher tariffs can be expected soon.
Demand is strong for capacity on virtually all routes, while a number of carriers, especially to the Far East, said they are turning away business.
And for the first time in 1996, there are also clear signs of the long-awaited recovery in westbound transatlantic traffic with volumes rising and capacity declining, the survey shows.

Roger Blacklock of the British International Freight Association (BIFA) said the latest available data suggests overall air cargo exports were up three percent from the start of the year by August/September, with growth to the U.S up nine percent.
"Overall September was a storming month, while October is going like a steam train," said one consolidator. "It is not just to the Far East, but also to the U.S," he added.
Rates to Tokyo are around 2.05 stg per kg compared with 1.97 stg previously, while substantially higher rates are available on some direct carriers.
Seoul is around 1.95 stg compared to the previous 1.85 with. Hong Kong is marginally firmer at 1.20 stg.

"Business to Japan is very good, with October continuing the strong trend seen in September," said Japan Airline's Tony Edwards. "The forecast for the next month and the next six months should be pretty good," he added.
At All Nippon Airways, activity "is buoyant and we're looking at a record month in October for both tonnage and revenue," since the service started in 1989, an ANA cargo source said.
The two Japanese airlines are moving respectively 150 tonnes and 250 tonnes a week of cargo.
Korean Airlines is planning a five pence a kg increase in its general rates from November 1, to 2.05 stg a kg for 100 kg, said the carrier's cargo manager, Frank Smith.
The rise comes against a background of strong two-way trade between the UK and Korea.

South east Asia is seeing a steady but high level of business, with rates to Singapore marginally firmer at 1.25 to 1.28 stg per kg for 100 kg, compared to a previous 1.24 stg. Australia has also firmed to 2.10 stg a kg from 2.07 stg.

Singapore Airlines cargo manager, Barry Gibson said "Right now we could use an extra freighter. On Monday we were already full till Friday. It is very good on all routes and we're turning some people away."

Business to Australia continues to grow steadily, he added. A cargo agent said "Australia has come in out of the blue and it is terribly difficult to find space," a development which he attributed to a more positive view of the country's economy and pre-Xmas traffic build-up.

Traffic volumes are again improving to the U.S, and the rise seems to be greater than the traditional last quarter upturn, industry sources said. At the same time available capacity is tightening as summer charter flights are being withdrawn, while seasonal headwinds can limit uplift on some routes.

Rates to New York's JFK are still around 0.62 stg a kg for 100 kg, although for complete dense pallets, some carriers are apparently quoting rates of less than half that figure reflecting the intense competition on the route. To Chicago, there is an upward drift to around 0.72 stg a kg from 0.68 stg, with Los Angeles at 0.73 stg from O.70 stg.
American Airlines cargo manager, John Smith said: "There is very strong demand from everywhere in Europe to both the U.S and Latin America. It's consistent to all destinations".
"Business has picked up and it is a very good October, with recent flights going out full," he added, while Sharon Wright of AMI said: " U.S. trade has been going very well since September".
And Northwest's cargo manager, Brian Mutton reported very busy westbound traffic, although this would be expected at this time of the year.
Rates to the southern U.S. states, including Florida, are expected to firm further with the withdrawal of the summer charter business which will reduce capacity by about 50 percent.
The Latin America market is also seeing strong ex-UK export demand with Brazil, Argentina, Chile and Mexico ranking as key destinations.
Average rates to Sao Paulo are steady at 2.06 stg a kg for 100 kgs, although indirect carriers transhipping via Miami are offering as low as 1.40 to 1.50 stg a kg, industry sources said.
Varig, which operates three times a week to Brazil with McDonnell Douglas MD-11s and twice with DC-10s is flying out full loads and yields are better than four to five months ago.

"We would normally expect to get become very busy at end-October, but this year it started in September," said a Varig source. "There has been no increase in rates, but these could come in December, if business continues at this pace," the source added.

The trend was confirmed by Enrique Sagra from Iberia "Business is very good, there is a big demand. There is not enough capacity and there's a seven to eight day delay for many destinations," he said.
"There are a lot of chemicals and pharmaceuticals moving to Sao Paulo at the moment," he said. Mexico is also a strong market from the UK and Europe, he added.

"And twice in the past 10 days, I've heard of agents offering the full IATA tariff rate for urgent shipments to Buenos Aires. That's about 50 percent over the market rate -- the last time I heard that was two years ago." Sagra said.

However a European carrier described business to Latin America as "reasonable but sustainable". He added that the busy passenger season is now starting and combined with headwinds, there will be additional cargo capacity constraints in the next few months.

American Airlines is seeing very firm demand for large cargoes for transhipment to Latin America via Miami but, "we don't have enough available capacity out of the U.S. at the moment", said cargo manager, John Smith.

The South African market is also experiencing the end-year upturn in volume, with more carriers and more flights than last year, "there is a lot more competitive pressure on prices" said an industry source.
Virgin Atlantic began scheduled passenger services to Johannesburg on October 2 using an Airbus A340 offering around 15 tonnes of cargo capacity per flight.

The average rate has eased to around 1.65 stg a kg for 100 kgs on quality direct services, but some major non-UK based cargo carriers are reportedly offering as low as 1.30 stg in an effort to generate uplift, he added.

Paul Rodwell,UK cargo manager for Alitalia, which offers daily flights to Johannesburg said however; "business is doing very well despite the increased capacity, especially at weekends. We're now targeting early and mid-week cargo movements."
And AMI's Wright added "business is doing well, although perhaps not as well as some routes" simply due to the increased capacity which is now available.

Rates to the Gulf are firmer at around 0.80 stg per kg for 100 kg to Dubai and 0.95 stg to Bahrain. A leading Gulf-based carrier source said ex-UK flights were going out full and shipments are very good at the moment.

"Onward traffic to Hong Kong and Singapore is also very busy. We've had a number of flights closed for cargo several days early," he added. - Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542 8982 Fax +44 171 542 5017
